title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
short_description: James Clear’s practical system for getting 1% better every day — identity, systems, the habit loop, and the Four Laws of Behavior Change.

questions.question_text: According to Atomic Habits, what do you 'fall to the level of'?
questions.option_b: Your systems

questions.question_text: What are the four steps of Clear’s habit loop?
questions.option_b: Cue, craving, response, reward

questions.question_text: What is the 1st law of behavior change for building a good habit?
questions.option_b: Make it rare

questions.question_text: What does Clear mean by identity-based habits?
questions.option_b: Focusing on who you want to become, with actions as votes for that identity

questions.question_text: How do you break a bad habit using Clear’s framework?
questions.option_b: Invert the Four Laws (e.g. make the cue invisible)

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey
short_description: Stephen R. Covey’s principle-centered classic: seven habits that move you from dependence to independence to interdependence.

questions.question_text: What is Habit 1 in Covey’s framework?
questions.option_b: Be Proactive

questions.question_text: Habits 1–3 are mainly about achieving what?
questions.option_b: Independence (private victory)

questions.question_text: What does 'Begin with the End in Mind' emphasize?
questions.option_b: A clear personal vision / mission before acting

questions.question_text: What is Habit 5?
questions.option_a: Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood
questions.option_b: Always speak first

questions.question_text: What does Sharpen the Saw mean?
questions.option_b: Renew physical, mental, social/emotional, and spiritual capacity
questions.option_c: Cut people out of your life

title: Think and Grow Rich
author: Napoleon Hill
short_description: Napoleon Hill’s classic success philosophy — burning desire, faith, auto-suggestion, specialized knowledge, organized planning, and the Master Mind.

questions.question_text: What does Hill say is the starting point of all achievement?
questions.option_b: A burning, definite desire

questions.question_text: What is auto-suggestion in Think and Grow Rich?
questions.option_b: Self-suggestion that influences the subconscious through emotionalized repetition

questions.question_text: According to Hill, what should you do if a plan fails?
questions.option_b: Replace the plan and continue

questions.question_text: What is the Master Mind principle?
questions.option_b: A harmonious alliance of minds toward a definite purpose

questions.question_text: How does Hill say faith can be strengthened?
questions.option_b: Through affirmation and repeated instructions to the subconscious

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
short_description: Morgan Housel’s essays on how behavior — not spreadsheets — drives financial outcomes: compounding, enough, room for error, and being reasonable.

questions.question_text: What does Housel argue matters more than pure financial brilliance?
questions.option_b: Behavior and temperament with money
questions.option_c: Knowing every tax loophole on day one

questions.question_text: Why is compounding 'confounding' in Housel’s telling?
questions.option_a: It only works for one year
questions.option_b: Its power is easy to underestimate and requires long, uninterrupted time
questions.option_d: It only applies to cash under a mattress

questions.question_text: What is 'room for error'?
questions.option_b: A margin of safety so you can survive when plans go wrong

questions.question_text: What danger comes from never defining 'enough'?
questions.option_b: Goalposts keep moving and risk-taking may never stop

questions.question_text: According to Housel, what can saving buy beyond purchases?
questions.option_b: Flexibility and control over your time

title: Can't Hurt Me
author: David Goggins
short_description: David Goggins’ memoir of mental toughness — the Accountability Mirror, Taking Souls, Cookie Jar, 40% Rule, and callousing the mind.

questions.question_text: What is the Accountability Mirror?
questions.option_b: A daily radical-honesty practice facing your real gaps and goals

questions.question_text: What is the Cookie Jar for Goggins?
questions.option_b: A mental stockpile of past victories and survived hardships

questions.question_text: What does the 40% Rule claim?
questions.option_a: You should only ever use 40% effort
questions.option_b: When your mind says you’re done, you may still have substantial capacity left

questions.question_text: What does 'callous the mind' mean in this book?
questions.option_b: Strengthen mental toughness by repeatedly doing hard things

questions.question_text: What does Goggins argue about most people’s capability usage?
questions.option_b: They often live far below their potential
questions.option_d: Limits are purely genetic and fixed

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
short_description: Cal Newport’s case for focused, distraction-free work — deep vs shallow, four rules, depth philosophies, and the shutdown ritual.

questions.question_text: How does Newport define deep work?
questions.option_b: Distraction-free concentration on cognitively demanding tasks

questions.question_text: Which depth philosophy uses a daily consistent block?
questions.option_b: Rhythmic

questions.question_text: What is Rule 2 in Deep Work?
questions.option_b: Embrace boredom to train focus

questions.question_text: What is a shutdown ritual for?
questions.option_b: Closing open loops and signaling the workday is done

questions.question_text: What does Newport say about deep work’s economic value?
questions.option_b: It is becoming more valuable while becoming rarer
questions.option_d: It is the same as shallow work

title: Mindset
author: Carol S. Dweck
short_description: Carol Dweck’s research on fixed vs growth mindset — how beliefs about ability shape challenge-seeking, effort, failure, praise, and resilience.

questions.question_text: What is a fixed mindset?
questions.option_a: Belief that abilities can always grow
questions.option_b: Belief that qualities like intelligence are largely static
questions.option_c: Belief that effort never matters for anyone
questions.option_d: Belief that feedback is always wrong

questions.question_text: What is a growth mindset?
questions.option_b: Belief that abilities can be developed through effort, strategies, and learning

questions.question_text: How does a growth mindset typically view failure?
questions.option_b: As painful but useful information for improvement
questions.option_c: As proof you should quit forever

questions.question_text: What kind of praise better supports growth, according to Dweck’s research themes?
questions.option_b: Praising process: strategies, practice, and persistence

questions.question_text: What is a risk of a 'false' growth mindset?
questions.option_b: Praising effort alone without better strategies and real learning

title: The Power of Now
author: Eckhart Tolle
short_description: Eckhart Tolle’s guide to presence — disidentifying from egoic thinking, psychological time, the pain-body, and returning to the Now.

questions.question_text: What does Tolle say is ultimately real and primary for peace?
questions.option_b: The present moment (the Now)

questions.question_text: What is psychological time in Tolle’s teaching?
questions.option_b: Living absorbed in past/future mental stories rather than the present

questions.question_text: What is the pain-body?
questions.option_b: Accumulated emotional pain that can activate and feed on negativity

questions.question_text: How does presence affect identification with pain?
questions.option_b: Observing without becoming the pain withdraws identification
questions.option_c: It requires arguing with every thought
questions.option_d: It means suppressing all feeling forever

questions.question_text: Which practice fits Tolle’s approach?
questions.option_b: Anchoring attention in breath / inner body / present sensing

title: The Mountain Is You
author: Brianna Wiest
short_description: Brianna Wiest on transforming self-sabotage into self-mastery — internal mountains, triggers, emotional intelligence, identity death, and discomfort.

questions.question_text: How does Wiest reframe self-sabotage?
questions.option_b: As often a form of self-protection that outlived its usefulness

questions.question_text: What is the 'mountain' in the book’s metaphor?
questions.option_b: Primarily internal obstacles and patterns you must climb through

questions.question_text: What do emotional triggers offer, according to this book’s themes?
questions.option_b: Information about wounds, beliefs, and needs

questions.question_text: Why is discomfort important in Wiest’s framing?
questions.option_b: Avoiding discomfort can mean avoiding the life you want
questions.option_d: Discomfort means you chose wrong forever

questions.question_text: What attitude does the book favor toward changing sabotage patterns?
questions.option_b: Understanding plus responsibility and new aligned action

title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
author: Mark Manson
short_description: Mark Manson’s counterintuitive guide to values — the backwards law, Feedback Loop from Hell, choosing what to care about, and responsibility over fault.

questions.question_text: What is the Feedback Loop from Hell?
questions.option_b: Feeling bad, then judging yourself for feeling bad, which multiplies suffering

questions.question_text: What does Manson say about 'not giving a f*ck'?
questions.option_b: Selectively care about what truly matters; stop wasting care everywhere

questions.question_text: Which are closer to Manson’s 'good values'?
questions.option_a: Always being right and endless pleasure-chasing
questions.option_b: Honesty, curiosity, and responsibility

questions.question_text: What is the fault vs responsibility distinction?
questions.option_b: You may not be at fault for an event, but you are responsible for your response
questions.option_c: Responsibility means blaming yourself for everything
questions.option_d: Fault means you must fix others

questions.question_text: What is the backwards law idea in the book?
questions.option_a: Wanting only positivity can create more negativity; accepting struggle can help
questions.option_b: Always avoid hard things

title: Grit
author: Angela Duckworth
short_description: Angela Duckworth’s research on grit: passion plus perseverance, effort counting twice, and the four psychological assets that build staying power.

questions.question_text: What is Duckworth’s definition of grit?
questions.option_b: Passion plus perseverance for long-term goals

questions.question_text: In Duckworth’s formula, why does effort 'count twice'?
questions.option_b: Talent × effort = skill, and skill × effort = achievement

questions.question_text: Which four psychological assets does Duckworth link to growing grit?
questions.option_b: Interest, practice, purpose, and hope

questions.question_text: What characterizes deliberate practice?
questions.option_a: Only repeating easy skills for fun
questions.option_b: Stretch goals, concentration, feedback, and refinement

questions.question_text: What does the Grit Scale primarily measure?
questions.option_b: Consistency of interests and perseverance of effort

title: The Compound Effect
author: Darren Hardy
short_description: Darren Hardy on how small, smart choices compound into massive results — habits, momentum, influences, and acceleration.

questions.question_text: What is the core idea of The Compound Effect?
questions.option_b: Small smart choices + consistency + time create massive results

questions.question_text: Why does Hardy emphasize tracking choices?
questions.option_b: To reveal patterns self-deception hides

questions.question_text: What is 'Big Mo' in Hardy’s framework?
questions.option_b: Momentum created by consistent action

questions.question_text: Which three influence categories does Hardy highlight?
questions.option_b: Input, associations, and environment

questions.question_text: When does Hardy say you should accelerate?
questions.option_b: When results appear and the flywheel is already turning

title: The Four Agreements
author: Don Miguel Ruiz
short_description: Don Miguel Ruiz’s Toltec-inspired code: be impeccable with your word, don’t take anything personally, don’t make assumptions, and always do your best.

questions.question_text: What is the first agreement?
questions.option_b: Be impeccable with your word

questions.question_text: What does 'don’t take anything personally' mean?
questions.option_b: Others’ actions reflect them more than your worth

questions.question_text: How does Ruiz suggest you avoid assumptions?
questions.option_b: Ask questions and communicate clearly

questions.question_text: What is true of 'always do your best'?
questions.option_a: Your best is identical every day
questions.option_b: Your best changes with circumstances; sincerity matters

questions.question_text: In Ruiz’s framing, what does childhood 'domestication' create?
questions.option_b: Unconscious fear-based agreements and inner judgment

title: Ikigai
author: Héctor García & Francesc Miralles
short_description: García and Miralles on the Japanese idea of ikigai — a reason for being — and habits linked to longevity, flow, and joyful purpose.

questions.question_text: What does ikigai roughly mean?
questions.option_b: A reason for being / reason to get up

questions.question_text: What eating principle is associated with Okinawan longevity in the book?
questions.option_b: Hara hachi bu — stop around 80% full

questions.question_text: How is flow related to ikigai?
questions.option_b: Absorbing challenge-skill balance reveals and fuels meaningful engagement

questions.question_text: What do the authors suggest about retirement?
questions.option_b: Stay active with purpose rather than abandoning contribution

questions.question_text: Which is one of the ten rules of ikigai?
questions.option_b: Live in the moment / follow your ikigai

title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie
short_description: Dale Carnegie’s timeless classic on human relations — appreciation, genuine interest, names, listening, and leading without resentment.

questions.question_text: What does Carnegie advise instead of criticizing first?
questions.option_b: Avoid criticism/condemnation/complaint; use sincere appreciation and better framing

questions.question_text: Why does Carnegie emphasize a person’s name?
questions.option_a: Names are legally required in chat
questions.option_b: A person’s name is deeply important to them; remembering it shows respect

questions.question_text: What is meant by arousing an 'eager want'?
questions.option_b: Frame requests in terms of the other person’s interests and desires

questions.question_text: How should you handle being wrong, according to Carnegie?
questions.option_b: Admit it quickly and emphatically

questions.question_text: What is a key leadership principle for correcting others?
questions.option_a: Humiliate them publicly so they learn
questions.option_b: Praise first, save face, encourage improvement, invite ownership

title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
author: Eric Jorgenson
short_description: Eric Jorgenson’s curated guide to Naval Ravikant’s thinking on wealth, specific knowledge, leverage, judgment, and happiness.

questions.question_text: How does Naval distinguish wealth from status?
questions.option_b: Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep; status is zero-sum social rank
questions.option_d: Wealth is only cash in a wallet

questions.question_text: What is specific knowledge?
questions.option_a: Whatever a standard school course teaches everyone
questions.option_b: Unique, hard-to-train knowledge that feels like play to you

questions.question_text: Which leverage forms does Naval call more permissionless?
questions.option_b: Code and media

questions.question_text: Why is judgment so important in Naval’s framework?
questions.option_b: Leverage amplifies decisions, so clear thinking becomes extremely valuable

questions.question_text: How does Naval frame happiness?
questions.option_b: As a skill related to peace, presence, and managing desire — aided by meditation

title: The One Thing
author: Gary Keller
short_description: Gary Keller’s focus classic: the Focusing Question, successive dominoes, time blocking, and going small to achieve big results.

questions.question_text: What is Keller’s Focusing Question aimed at finding?
questions.option_a: Every task on a long list
questions.option_b: The one action that makes everything else easier or unnecessary
questions.option_d: What others want you to do first

questions.question_text: What does 'go small' mean in The One Thing?
questions.option_b: Narrow focus to the highest-leverage priority to achieve big results

questions.question_text: Why does Keller emphasize time blocking?
questions.option_b: To protect a non-negotiable period for the ONE Thing before interruptions win
questions.option_c: To fill the day with meetings

questions.question_text: What is the domino metaphor about?
questions.option_b: Lining up priorities so successive successes unlock larger outcomes

questions.question_text: When should you typically do your ONE Thing, per Keller’s willpower view?
questions.option_b: When willpower and energy are freshest — often early

title: 12 Rules for Life
author: Jordan B. Peterson
short_description: Jordan B. Peterson’s practical-philosophical rules for meaning and responsibility — posture, self-care, truth, precision, and aiming up.

questions.question_text: What is the practical point of 'stand up straight with your shoulders back'?
questions.option_b: Face life with embodied readiness; posture and willingness affect feedback and confidence

questions.question_text: What does Rule 2 ask you to do?
questions.option_b: Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping

questions.question_text: According to Rule 4, whom should you compare yourself to?
questions.option_b: Who you were yesterday, not everyone else today

questions.question_text: What should you do before criticizing the world (Rule 6)?
questions.option_b: Set your house in order / stop doing what you know is wrong

questions.question_text: What do Rules 8 and 10 emphasize together?
questions.option_b: Tell the truth and be precise in your speech

title: Outliers
author: Malcolm Gladwell
short_description: Malcolm Gladwell on why outliers succeed — 10,000 hours, hidden opportunity, cultural legacy, meaningful work, and the Matthew effect.

questions.question_text: What is Gladwell’s main critique of typical success stories?
questions.option_b: They ignore hidden advantages, timing, and culture — not only individual talent
questions.option_c: Only luck matters and effort is useless

questions.question_text: What does the 10,000-hour discussion emphasize?
questions.option_b: Enormous practice — and unusual access to practice opportunities

questions.question_text: What is the relative-age effect example in Outliers often about?
questions.option_b: Youth sports cutoff dates advantaging older children in a cohort

questions.question_text: What three qualities does Gladwell associate with meaningful work?
questions.option_b: Complexity, autonomy, and a link between effort and reward

questions.question_text: What is the Matthew effect in this context?
questions.option_a: Advantages compound — early gains attract more gains
questions.option_b: Everyone starts equal forever

title: Essentialism
author: Greg McKeown
short_description: Greg McKeown’s disciplined pursuit of less but better — explore, eliminate, execute, and protect the essential with sleep, play, and tradeoffs.

questions.question_text: What is Essentialism’s core phrase?
questions.option_b: Less but better

questions.question_text: What are the three phases McKeown emphasizes?
questions.option_b: Explore, eliminate, execute

questions.question_text: How should essentialists treat tradeoffs?
questions.option_b: Accept and choose them consciously — or others will choose for you
questions.option_c: Always say yes to avoid them
questions.option_d: Only make tradeoffs once a year

questions.question_text: Why does McKeown value sleep and play in exploration?
questions.option_b: They protect judgment and spark insight needed to discern essentials

questions.question_text: What is a practical elimination question for old commitments?
questions.option_b: If I didn’t already have this commitment, how hard would I work to get it?

title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
author: Robert Kiyosaki
short_description: A guide to financial literacy and wealth building — the principles that separate assets from liabilities and how to make money work for you.

questions.question_text: What is the main difference between an asset and a liability according to Rich Dad?
questions.option_a: Assets cost money, liabilities make money
questions.option_b: Assets put money in your pocket, liabilities take money out
questions.option_c: Assets are investments, liabilities are expenses

questions.question_text: What does "Mind Your Own Business" mean in the context of the book?
questions.option_a: Focus on your job and career
questions.option_b: Build assets outside of your profession

questions.question_text: According to Rich Dad, what should you prioritize when it comes to money?
questions.option_a: Working harder for a higher salary
questions.option_b: Learning financial literacy and building assets

questions.question_text: What is the "Rat Race" that Kiyosaki describes?
questions.option_b: The cycle of working to pay bills, which keeps you working

questions.question_text: What mindset shift does Rich Dad recommend instead of saying "I can't afford it"?
questions.option_a: Accept that you can't afford it
questions.option_b: Ask "How can I afford it?"
questions.option_d: Wait until you have more money
